title: Random Flip Matrix
statement:
Write a class `Solution` for a grid of `m` rows and `n` columns whose cells all start as `0`.

- `new Solution(m, n)` sets up the grid.
- `flip()` chooses one cell that is currently `0`, with every such cell equally likely, turns it into `1`, and returns its position `[i, j]` (row `i`, column `j`, both counted from `0`).
- `reset()` turns every cell back into `0`.

Each call to `flip()` is guaranteed to have at least one `0` cell available. The grid can hold up to 10^8 cells, so aim for small time and memory per call and for as few calls to the random generator as possible.

Use `Math.random()` for randomness; in this app it follows a fixed seed, so runs repeat exactly. Because many outputs are correct, an answer is accepted when the constructor and every `reset()` give `null`, every `flip()` returns an in-range cell that is still `0`, and over a case the chosen cells are spread across the free cells about as evenly as a fair choice would spread them (a generous statistical check).
constraints: Every call to flip finds at least one cell equal to 0
At most 1000 calls in total are made to flip and reset (at most 499 per case here)
notes:
## Intuition

Give every cell a number in row-major order: cell `[i, j]` is `i * n + j`, so the numbers run from `0` to `m * n - 1`. A fair flip must pick uniformly among the numbers still free. Drawing random cells and retrying when one is already `1` works, but it calls the random generator again and again once most cells are taken, and a real grid of 10^8 cells would not fit in memory.

The trick from the Fisher–Yates shuffle: imagine an array whose first `remaining` slots hold exactly the free numbers. Pick a random slot below `remaining`, return its number, then copy the number from the last free slot into the picked slot and shrink `remaining` by one. Every free number stays in the front part and each flip uses one random draw. Almost every slot still holds its own index, so a `Map` stores only the slots that were changed.

## Approach

1. The constructor stores `rows`, `cols`, sets `remaining = m * n` and starts an empty `moved` map (slot → number held there).
2. `flip()`: draw `pick` uniformly from `0 .. remaining - 1`, then decrease `remaining` so it names the last free slot.
3. `cell` is the number in slot `pick` (`moved` entry, or `pick` itself), and `last` is the number in slot `remaining`.
4. Store `last` in slot `pick`, so the number that was at the end stays reachable.
5. Turn `cell` back into a position: row `Math.floor(cell / cols)`, column `cell % cols`.
6. `reset()`: restore `remaining` and clear `moved`.

## Example 1, step by step

With `m = 3, n = 1` the numbers are `0, 1, 2`. Suppose the draws are `1, 1, 0, 2` (LeetCode's sample run):

- Flip 1: `pick = 1`, `remaining = 2`, `cell = 1`, `last = 2`, `moved = {1 → 2}`; return `[1, 0]`.
- Flip 2: `pick = 1`, `remaining = 1`, `cell = 2` (from `moved`), `last = 2`; return `[2, 0]`.
- Flip 3: `pick = 0`, `remaining = 0`, `cell = 0`; return `[0, 0]`.
- `reset()` empties `moved`; the next draw `2` returns `[2, 0]`.

The seeded run in this app makes different draws, which are just as valid.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1) expected per `flip()` (a few map operations); `reset()` is O(k) to clear k entries.
- Space: O(k), where k is the number of flips since the last reset; at most one map entry per flip.

## Pitfalls

- Allocating the grid or a list of all `m * n` numbers: up to 10^8 entries.
- Forgetting to clear `moved` in `reset()` leaves stale swaps, so a later flip can return a cell twice.
- Decode with the column count: `cell / cols` and `cell % cols`, not `rows`.
- Draw from `remaining`, not from `m * n`; drawing from the full range can land on a slot that holds no free number.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `rows`, `cols` | grid size `m` and `n` |
| `remaining` | how many cells are still `0`; slots `0 .. remaining - 1` hold them |
| `moved` | slots whose number differs from their own index |
| `pick` | the random slot chosen by this flip |
| `cell` | the number (row-major index) stored in slot `pick` |
| `last` | the number in the last free slot, moved into slot `pick` |

narration.3: Remember the number of rows for reset.
narration.4: Remember the number of columns, used to decode a cell number into a row and column.
narration.5: All m * n cells are free, so slots 0 .. m * n - 1 hold the free cell numbers.
narration.6: Only slots whose number was changed by a swap are stored; all others hold their own index.
narration.10: Draw one free slot uniformly at random: the only random call per flip.
narration.11: The free part shrinks by one; remaining now names its last slot.
narration.12: Read the cell number held in the picked slot (its own index unless it was swapped).
narration.13: Read the cell number held in the last free slot.
narration.14: Move that last number into the picked slot so it stays among the free cells.
narration.15: Turn the row-major cell number into [row, column].
narration.20: No slot is swapped any more, so forget all stored moves.
